title: The Thermal Micro-Environment Shapes T Cell Responses from Antigen Encounter to Cell Fate
content: Temperature is an important but underappreciated component of the immune microenvironment that can shape T cell responses during inflammation. While fever has traditionally been viewed primarily as a consequence of immune activation, accumulating evidence indicates that elevated temperature can directly influence T cell trafficking, antigen recognition, signaling, differentiation, and effector function. This review examines temperature as a dynamic physical dimension of T cell immunity, distinguishing systemic fever from localized inflammatory heat, or calor. We summarize evidence showing that fever can alter lymphocyte trafficking and antigen presentation, while temperature-dependent changes in membrane organization and receptor clustering can modulate T cell receptor signaling and activation. In peripheral tissues, local thermal changes may further influence integrin-mediated adhesion, transendothelial migration, antigen recognition, and effector function. Emerging evidence also suggests that thermal exposure can induce persistent metabolic and cellular changes, although its role in memory T cell formation remains unresolved. Overall, temperature represents an additional layer of immune regulation that interacts with antigenic, cytokine, and tissue-specific signals to shape T cell responses. Defining the thermal environments experienced by T cells in vivo will be important for understanding the physiological relevance of these effects.
